# Preparations

Load the necessary libraries

```{r}
#| label: libraries

library(tidyverse)     #for data wrangling etc
library(cmdstanr)      #for cmdstan
library(brms)          #for fitting models in STAN
library(coda)          #for diagnostics
library(bayesplot)     #for diagnostics
library(DHARMa)        #for residual diagnostics
library(rstan)         #for interfacing with STAN

```

# Scenario

Here is a modified example from @Quinn-2002-2002. Day and Quinn
(1989) described an experiment that examined how rock surface type
affected the recruitment of barnacles to a rocky shore. The experiment
had a single factor, surface type, with 4 treatments or levels: algal
species 1 (ALG1), algal species 2 (ALG2), naturally bare surfaces (NB)
and artificially scraped bare surfaces (S). There were 5 replicate plots
for each surface type and the response (dependent) variable was the
number of newly recruited barnacles on each plot after 4 weeks.

![Six-plated barnacle](../resources/barnacles.jpg){#fig-barnacle width="224" height="308"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

TREAT   BARNACLE
------- ----------
ALG1    27
..      ..
ALG2    24
..      ..
NB      9
..      ..
S       12
..      ..

: Format of day.csv data files {#tbl-day .table-condensed}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

-------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**TREAT**      Categorical listing of surface types. ALG1 = algal species 1, ALG2 = algal species 2, NB = naturally bare surface, S = scraped bare surface.
**BARNACLE**   The number of newly recruited barnacles on each plot after 4 weeks.
-------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

: Description of the variables in the day data file {#tbl-day1 .table-condensed}

:::
::::

# Read in the data

```{r}
#| label: readData

day <- read_csv('../data/day.csv', trim_ws = TRUE)
```



Start by declaring the categorical variables as factor.


Model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{Pois}(\lambda_i)\\
ln(\mu_i) &= \boldsymbol{\beta} \bf{X_i}\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(3.1, 0.3)\\
\beta_{1,2,3} &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0,1)\\
\end{align}
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ is a vector of effects parameters and $\bf{X}$ is a model matrix representing the intercept and treatment contrasts for the effects of Treatment on barnacle recruitment.

# Exploratory data analysis
```{r}
#| label: boxplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#no assumptions with Poisson but do need to pay attention to how many 0s there are

day |> ggplot(aes(y = BARNACLE, x = TREAT)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_point(color = 'red')

#no zeros
#nothing stands out as looking "wrong" --> can move ahead
```

# Fit the model
```{r}
#| label: set categorical predictor as factor
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day <- day |> 
  mutate(TREAT = factor(TREAT))
```

```{r}
#| label: model formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_form <- bf(BARNACLE ~ TREAT, family = poisson(link = 'log'))
```

```{r}
#| label: priors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

get_prior(day_form, data = day)
#can set a seperate prior for each beta
#OR set one for everything

#for Intercept look at the median of ALG1 (since that is what the intercept comes from)
day |> 
  group_by(TREAT) |> 
  summarise(median(log(BARNACLE)), mad(log(BARNACLE))) #need to use log because we have the logit link function for a Poisson distribution (couldn't do this if we had zeros)

#intercept and all betas
priors <- prior(normal(3.1,0.3), class = 'Intercept') +
  prior(normal(0,0.4), class = 'b') #keep mean at 0 because we want to let the data decide, variance will be something big enough to include all of the mad() variances

```

# MCMC sampling diagnostics
```{r}
#| label: prior only model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

#stan uses no u turn sampler (NUTS)
day_brm2 <- brm(day_form,
                 data=day,
                 prior=priors,
                 sample_prior="only",
                 iter=5000,
                 chains=3, cores=3, #one core per chain
                 warmup=1000,
                 thin=5,
                 backend="cmdstanr",
                 refresh=0, 
                 seed = 1)

```

```{r}
#| label: plot model day_brm2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm2 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#larger black dot is estimated mean of posterior
#error bars are CI lower and upper --> 95% represent TYPICAL recruitment not alllll recruitment
```

```{r}
#| label: sample from prior and data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

day_brm3 <- update(day_brm2, sample_prior = 'yes', refresh = 0, seed = 1)

```
```{r}
#| label: plot model day_brm3
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#now model looks much more refined
#and looks like data is driving the trend, not priors which is what we want
```

```{r}
#| label: examine all priors and posteriors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3 |> SUYR_prior_and_posterior()

#proof that priors are influential (thats what we want)
#this function helps show you what prior is problematic

#there's no way b posterior is the same as the prior, so no way priors are driving the trends
```
# Model validation
```{r}
#| label: traceplots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3$fit |> stan_trace()

day_brm3$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: autocorrelation plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3$fit |> stan_ac()
#standard to have a bar at 0
#at a lag of 1 (x-axis) we don't want to have large autocorrelation --> no bias between draws
#therefore, thinning was adequate
```

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#how well did chains converge
day_brm3$fit |> stan_rhat()
#want values <1.01
#if they are above 1.01 then the chains were different from each other
      # ^ might need to add more iterations or check priors 
```

```{r}
#| label: effective sample size
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3$fit |> stan_ess()

#uses no u turn sampler (NUTS) --> not your actual data
#tells us how many draws were effective out of all of them
#want this to be >0.5, and closer to 1 the better
#its okay if they are <0.5, but this means the model isn't efficient and the priors were probably too large,
#causing the sampler to go too far
```

```{r}
#| label: posterior probs density overlay
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3 |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)

#dark line is actual distribution of our data
#our model reconstructs the data quite well
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

preds <- day_brm3 |> posterior_predict(ndraws=250, summary=FALSE)
day.resids <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse = t(preds),
                            observedResponse = day$BARNACLE,
                            fittedPredictedResponse = apply(preds, 2, median),
                            integerResponse = TRUE)
day.resids |> plot()

#QQ Plot: plots quantiles (median, upper, lower, etc)
#straight line applies that residuals follow nominated distribution (normal in this case)
#you want straight line
#KS: Smirnoff test for conformity to distribution --> if it was significant, maybe pay attention to it and see if you can change anything --> but don't blindly accept this
#Dispersion: ratio of variance to the mean --> for normal distribution we want close to 1
#Outlier test: if in red, check and see if it really is a problem

#residual plot: dont want any patterns (fan shape = unequal variances)

#need to test Poisson assumption that dispersion = 1
testDispersion(day.resids)
#we want red line to be near the peak of the simulated data (histogram peak) --> looks good!
#to the right = overdispersion
#to the left = underdispersed
```
# Partial effects plots
```{r}
#| label: partial effects plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3 |> conditional_effects() |> plot(points = TRUE)
```

# Model investigation
```{r}
#| label: simple summary
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#this is on log scale so not helpful
day_brm3 |> summary()

#need to exp()
exp(3.08) #this is the mean # of new recruits in ALG1

#diff between ALG1 and ALG2
exp(0.26) #but when you exp() it becomes multiplicative not additive so its 1.3 times greater than 21.8
exp(3.08 + 0.26) #this gives you the mean of ALG2
(1.29 - 1) * 100 #recruitment is 29% higher in the ALG2 group than the ALG1 group

#diff between ALG1 and NB
exp(-0.34)
(0.71 - 1) * 100 #29% decline

#PROBABILITY SCALE:
# >0.85 = evidence for that is weak
# <0.85 = no evidence at all
# >0.9 = there is evidence
# >0.95 = the evidence is strong
```

```{r}
#| label: table on log odds scale
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_brm3 |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*")) |> 
  exp() |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than ALG1
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than ALG1

#summary gives mean BUT this gives us the MEDIAN which is more robust

#our table is expentiated and exp(0) = 1 so that's why we use 1 in the calculation of P

# very strong evidence for recruitment being higher in ALG2 than ALG1 because lower and upper don't overlap with 1 (look at Pg column, Pg = 0.979)
# very strong evidence for recruitment being lower in NB than ALG1 because lower and upper don't overlap with 1 (Pl = 0.99)
# very strong evidence for recruitment being lower in S than ALG1 because lower and upper don't overlap with 1 (Pl = 1.00)

day_brm3 |> bayes_R2(summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 66% of variation in recruits can be explained by treatment
```

# Further investigations

```{r}
#| label: pairwise tests between treatments
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#don't need to create newdata for categorical data
day_table <- day_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~TREAT, type = "response") |> 
  pairs(reverse = TRUE) |> 
  tidy_draws() |> 
  exp() |>  #need to undo logit scale
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than ALG1
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than ALG1

#no evidence of a difference in recruitment between NB and S
```

# Summary Figure
```{r}
#| label: catepillar plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#y = variable, x = median
#linerange for error bars

catepillar_plot <- day_table |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = variable, x = median)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper)) +
  scale_x_continuous("Effect size (fold scale)", trans = scales::log2_trans(),
                     breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5))

#using a log2 scale to make the scale more intuitive than a linear scale
#2 and 0.5 would be the same distance away from 1. Doubling is the reverse of halving
log2(2) #1
log2(0.5) #-1
```

```{r}
#| label: ridge plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#first need to create a table with posterior draws/distribution
day_post <- day_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~TREAT) |> 
  pairs(reverse = TRUE) |> 
  gather_emmeans_draws() |> 
  mutate(pred = exp(.value))

#now ridge plots
day_post |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = pred)) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(aes(y = contrast,
                                   fill = factor(stat(x < 1.1 & x > 0.9))), #ROPE: region of practical equivalence. 10% is standard but can change it and justify why
                               alpha = 0.4, colour = 'white',
                               quantile_lines = TRUE,
                               quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
                               show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous("Effect size (fold scale)", trans = scales::log2_trans(),
                     breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5))

#if majority of distribution is in ROPE, there is evidence of no effect OR you need more power (more samples)

#prettier plot
ridge_plot <- day_post |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = pred)) +
  geom_density_ridges_gradient(aes(y = contrast,
                                   fill = factor(stat(x < 1.1 & x > 0.9))),
                               alpha = 0.4, colour = 'white',
                               quantile_lines = TRUE,
                               quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
                               show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous("Effect size (fold scale)", trans = scales::log2_trans(),
                     breaks = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5)) +
  scale_y_discrete("") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  theme_classic()

catepillar_plot / ridge_plot
```

```{r}
#| label: contrasts
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

cmat <- cbind('Alg2vsAlg1' = c(-1,1,0,0),
              'AlgvsBare' = c(0.5,0.5,-0.5,-0.5),
              'AlgvsNB' = c(0.5,0.5,-1,0))
cmat

day_brm3 |> emmeans(~TREAT, type = "response") |> 
  contrast(method = list(TREAT = cmat)) |> 
  tidy_draws() |> 
  exp() |>  #need to undo logit scale
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  Pl = ~mean(.x < 1), #less than ALG1
                  Pg = ~mean(.x > 1)) #greater than ALG1

#69% more recruitment on the algae surfaces vs the bare surfaces
#60% more recruitment on the algae surfaces vs the natural bare

#now to get absolute change
#the order of the backtransformation (regrid or exp) in relation to contrast matters
#back transformation after contrast is fractional scale
#back transformation before contrast is absolute scale
day_abs <- day_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~TREAT) |> 
  regrid() |> 
  contrast(method = list(TREAT = cmat)) |> 
  tidy_draws() |> 
  summarise_draws(median, HDInterval::hdi, Pl = ~mean(.x < 0), Pg = ~mean(.x >0))
```

# Final figure
```{r}
#| label: summary figure
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

day_em2 <- day_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~TREAT, type = "response") |>
  as.data.frame()
  
day_plot <- day_em2 |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = rate, x = TREAT)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = lower.HPD, ymax = upper.HPD))

day_plot + ridge_plot & theme_classic() #apply same theme to both plots
```
